problems.title: The published pooled-span Gaussian KL penalty differs from the released tokenwise MSE objective
problems.source_location: Section 4, Query Projection with KL Constraint, PDF p. 7.
claim: Paraphrase: in Query Projection with KL Constraint, Section 4, p. 7, the last-layer representations are pooled over each contiguous B/I span and compared with the corresponding pooled frozen teacher representation through a Gaussian KL penalty. Footnote 3 identifies mean pooling. The displayed formula is unnumbered. With \(N_+\) spans and \(m_s\) tokens in span \(s\), it is
\[L_{\mathrm{paper}}=\frac1{N_+}\sum_{s=1}^{N_+} \frac{\|\bar h_s-\bar t_s\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2},\qquad \bar h_s=\frac1{m_s}\sum_{k\in s}h_k,\quad \bar t_s=\frac1{m_s}\sum_{k\in s}t_k.\]
analysis: For one two-token span, let student vectors be \((1,0),(-1,0)\) and teacher vectors both zero. The pooled means agree, so the paper's penalty is \(0\), while tokenwise MSE is positive. In general tokenwise MSE adds the within-span variance of the student–teacher deviations. Changing a scalar loss weight cannot remove that extra term.

For dimension \(d=2\) and \(\sigma=1\), the current elementwise-mean loss gives \(1/4\) for that span. Generally it equals the pooled penalty divided by \(d\), plus \((2\sigma^2md)^{-1}\sum_k\|\Delta_k-\bar\Delta\|^2\). This extra nonnegative within-span variance term is structural, while one-token and constant-displacement spans are matching controls up to dimensional scaling.
result: The current release penalizes token-level variation absent from the stated pooled objective; the actually trained objective and resulting benchmark effect remain untraced.
repair: Either pool each student and teacher span first and sum squared coordinate differences as stated, or document the actual tokenwise feature-averaged loss and its extra variance term. Any change of loss scale needs separate empirical assessment.
problems.impact_rationale: The current release penalizes token-level variation absent from the stated pooled objective; the actually trained objective and resulting benchmark effect remain untraced.

problems.title: Image-balanced macro-gIoU does not establish improved segmentation of rare part classes
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Segmentation Evaluation, PDF p. 6; Appendix C.2–C.3, PDF p. 18.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 3.3, Segmentation Evaluation, p. 6, defines micro-gIoU by averaging all part-mask IoUs and macro-gIoU by first averaging within each image, then averaging the image means. The text interprets the latter as less affected by common parts. Appendix C.2-C.3, p. 18, attributes reported macro advantages to rare or uncommon part performance.

The released evaluator confirms the averaging unit: src/evaluation/evaluators/masks.py, lines 47-74, appends one mean per update in the macro branch and all paired mask IoUs in the micro branch. No part-class label is used for this reduction.
analysis: Averaging first by image equalizes image weights, not part-class frequencies. With one mask in each of ten images, nine common-class successes can dominate a complete rare-class failure in the tenth image. Therefore a higher image-macro gIoU need not imply better rare-class performance. The metric remains well defined and useful for image balancing.

An explicit ranking reversal uses nine common-class masks and one rare-class mask, one per image. Model A has IoUs \(1\) on common masks and \(0\) on the rare mask; model B has \(7/9\) and \(1\). Image-macro favors A, \(0.9>0.8\), while rare-class performance favors B, \(0<1\), and class-macro favors B, \(1/2<8/9\). Binary masks on a nine-pixel ground truth realize all values.
result: Metric-inference clarification; the metric itself is well defined.
repair: Interpret the current metric as a mean of per-image mask IoUs. Tie stronger rare-part conclusions to explicitly defined class identities, frequencies and class-stratified results.
problems.impact_rationale: Image weighting cannot identify rare-class improvement; the existing image-balanced metric remains valid for its stated aggregation unit.
problems.existing_correction_status: The existing objective or interpretation proposal remains applicable to current v3/current-head source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: Several comparative conclusions in Appendix C do not follow from its own printed tables
problems.source_location: Appendix C.1–C.3, PDF p. 18; Tables 9–11, PDF pp. 18–19.
claim: Appendix C.1-C.3, p. 18, makes stronger statements than some entries in Tables 9-11, pp. 18-19, support. The relevant claims, paraphrased, concern uniform superiority over the zero-shot baselines, a maximum two-point micro-gIoU gap after finetuning, and a macro-gIoU advantage used to diagnose another model’s treatment of uncommon parts.

This analysis checks these as substantive claims about comparative performance. It does not count numerical formatting, spelling, or table-caption mistakes as errata. The mismatch matters because it can reverse which method is favored on a task.
analysis: The appendix's uniform-superiority wording has a PartImageNet Intersection-macro exception. Its claimed maximum micro-gIoU deficit of two points is also contradicted by the PACO comparison, whose gap is \(3.8\) points. The macro result alone cannot diagnose another model's rare-class behavior, for the image-versus-class averaging reason in the preceding problem. These are corrections to conclusions drawn from the printed tables, not new performance measurements.

Current Table 10 gives PLUM \(12.2\) versus PixelLM \(12.8\) for zero-shot PartImageNet Intersection macro, and finetuned Difference macro \(60.7\) versus GLaMM \(65.4\), reversing the asserted advantage. Current Table 9 gives finetuned PACO Difference micro \(32.2\) versus PixelLM \(36.0\), a gap of \(3.8\), exceeding the stated two-point limit. Favorable cells remain; no new IoUs or significance test were computed.
result: Narrow the appendix comparisons to their individual printed wins and losses. No new significance test or overall ranking is established.
repair: A correction supported by the printed evidence is: PLUM leads most zero-shot segmentation comparisons in these tables, with a PartImageNet Intersection-macro exception; after finetuning it leads the six Identification/Intersection macro cells, while its micro-gIoU gap reaches \(3.8\) points on PACO. Difference-macro results depend on the dataset and comparator. They do not establish uniform dominance or a per-class diagnosis.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: Specific current table entries contradict universal superiority and maximum-gap summaries, while most zero-shot comparisons still favor PLUM.
problems.existing_correction_status: The existing objective or interpretation proposal remains applicable to current v3/current-head source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: Zero-shot requires the stated training-stage qualification; it does not mean absence of part-mask supervision
problems.source_location: Section 5, Implementation Details, PDF p. 7; Appendix A.1, PDF pp. 15–16; Appendix C.1, PDF p. 18.
claim: Section 5, Implementation Details, p. 7, explicitly defines the zero-shot baseline as the checkpoint after initial adaptation on a mixture that includes PACO-LVIS, Pascal Parts, and PartImageNet, before further PARTONOMY task finetuning. Appendix A.1, pp. 15-16, also describes this preliminary training stage. In contrast, Appendix C.1, p. 18, includes a statement that PLUM uses no part masks during pretraining.
analysis: The source qualifies zero-shot by training/evaluation stage. Prior part-mask supervision is compatible with that narrower usage; it is only incompatible with an unqualified claim of no part-mask training. Retaining the stated qualification resolves the apparent contradiction.
result: No additional error established beyond terminology scope.
problems.impact_rationale: The main text and current script explicitly define zero-shot relative to additional PARTONOMY finetuning, resolving the apparent claim of no earlier part-mask supervision.
problems.existing_correction_status: The stage-specific qualification is already present; no paper repair is proposed.

impact_rationale: The current regularizer differs from pooled-span KL, and image-balanced metrics and table summaries warrant local qualifications. The benchmark and PLUM’s overall gains are not invalidated; stage-specific zero-shot usage is preserved as a cleared concern.
